lessons.title: The parts of a grapevine
lessons.html:
Know the vine

A grapevine is a climbing plant. In a vineyard we train it on posts and wires (a trellis) so it grows in a neat shape. If you know the parts of the vine, you can follow instructions for pruning, tying and harvesting.

Parts below the ground

  • Roots hold the vine in the soil. They take up water and food from the soil. They also store food for the winter.

Parts above the ground

  • Trunk: the main stem. It carries water up and food down.
  • Cordons (arms): the woody arms that grow out along the wire.
  • Spurs: short pieces of last year's cane, left at pruning with a few buds.
  • Canes: one-year-old shoots that have turned brown and woody.
  • Shoots: the green new growth in spring. Shoots carry leaves, tendrils and bunches.
  • Buds: small bumps on the cane. In spring each bud can grow into a shoot.
  • Leaves: they use sunlight to make food (sugar) for the vine and the grapes.
  • Tendrils: thin curly parts that hold on to wires.
  • Bunches: first they are flowers, then small green berries, then ripe grapes.

Grafted vines

Almost all vines in South Africa are grafted. A small insect called phylloxera lives in the soil and attacks the roots of wine grape vines. So the vine is made of two parts:

  • The rootstock: the bottom part with roots. It resists phylloxera and suits the soil.
  • The scion: the top part. It gives the grape type (cultivar), for example Chenin blanc, Cabernet Sauvignon, Pinotage, or a table grape such as Crimson Seedless.

The place where the two parts join is the graft union. It looks like a swelling low on the trunk. Shoots that grow from the rootstock below the graft are called suckers. They must be removed, because they do not give the right grapes.

The vine's year

In winter the vine rests and has no leaves. In spring (about September) the buds burst. In late spring the vine flowers. In summer the berries grow and ripen. Harvest is from about January to April in the Western Cape. After harvest the leaves fall and the vine rests again.

lessons.title: Choosing and preparing a vineyard site
lessons.html:
A vineyard lasts many years

A new vineyard can produce for 20 years or more. Mistakes made at the start are hard to fix later. So the farmer plans carefully before planting.

What the farmer looks at

  • Climate: how hot, how cold, how much rain and wind. Some cultivars like cool places, others like warm places.
  • Slope and aspect: which way the land faces changes how much sun it gets.
  • Soil: depth, drainage, stones, and how much water it holds. Soil samples are sent to a laboratory.
  • Water: is there enough water for irrigation?
  • Market: who will buy the grapes, for wine, table grapes, or raisins?

Preparing the soil

  1. Remove old vines and roots. Old roots can carry diseases and pests.
  2. Rest the land, often with a cover crop, for a season or more.
  3. Deep soil preparation: the soil is ripped or ploughed deep with a big tractor. This breaks hard layers so roots can grow down.
  4. Add lime and fertiliser as the soil test says. Lime fixes acid soil. It is worked deep into the soil before planting, because it is hard to add later.
  5. Drainage: where water stands, drains may be put in.
  6. Make ridges in some soils so roots do not stand in water.

Choosing the rootstock and cultivar

The farmer chooses a rootstock that suits the soil. For example, some rootstocks handle dry soils better; others suit wet or rich soils. The cultivar must suit the climate and the market. Vines are bought from a registered nursery, so they are healthy and true to type.

Planning the rows

The farmer decides row direction, the space between rows (so tractors can pass) and the space between vines in the row. Rows are often planted north to south so both sides of the row get sun.

lessons.title: Planting and the trellis
lessons.html:
Planting young vines

Vines are usually planted in winter or early spring, while they are dormant (resting).

Caring for vines before planting

  • Keep vines cool, in the shade, and keep the roots moist. Dry roots die quickly.
  • Do not let vines lie in the sun on the land.
  • Trim roots and the top only as your supervisor shows you.

Planting steps

  1. Rows and vine positions are marked with a line, a measuring tape or GPS.
  2. Dig a hole big enough for the roots. Spread the roots out; do not bend them up.
  3. Plant at the right depth. The graft union must stay above the soil. If the scion touches soil, it can grow its own roots and phylloxera can attack them.
  4. Fill in soil and press it firmly to remove air pockets.
  5. Water the vine straight away.
  6. Put a stake next to the vine, and a grow tube or protector if the farm uses them.

The trellis

The trellis holds the vine up. It has:

  • End posts: strong posts at each end of the row, held with anchors.
  • Line posts: posts along the row.
  • Cordon wire: the wire where the arms of the vine grow.
  • Foliage wires: higher wires that hold the shoots up.

Common systems in South Africa include the vertical shoot position (VSP) trellis for wine grapes and overhead or gable systems for table grapes. Some vines are grown as bush vines without a trellis.

Safety

  • Wear gloves when working with wire. Wire under tension can whip back and cut you.
  • Wear safety boots. Watch for holes and stay clear of tractors and post drivers.
  • Drink water and rest in the shade on hot days.

Key points

  • A vine has a rootstock and a scion joined at the graft union.
  • Remove suckers that grow from the rootstock.
  • Good soil preparation before planting is very important.
  • Keep vine roots moist and cool before planting.
  • Plant with the graft union above the soil and water at once.
